sourceBindings.text: Use the three real sample results from the previous steps, or clearly labelled model values for practice. A texture class offers a clue about water, nutrients and workability. It does not, by itself, prove a field's drainage, salinity, crop suitability or amendment requirement.
Compare sandy and clay-rich soils for infiltration, water retention, nutrient retention, aeration and workability; explain the particle-and-pore reasoning and the influence of structure.
Interpret the supplied A/B/C model and your own separately identified results, giving conditional crop and management options with site evidence still needed.
Explain two likely challenges and one possible advantage of a clay-rich field, and reject automatic gypsum or a claim that compost changes the mineral texture class.

sourceBindings.text: A farmer describes a field as clay and asks what to do.
Possible challenge 1: sticky soil and poor field access when wet.
Possible challenge 2: low aeration or slow drainage when the actual structure and profile restrict water movement.
Possible advantage: charged clay surfaces can retain calcium and potassium cations.
Next action: check the actual drainage, structure and relevant soil tests before choosing an amendment.
State evidence and conditions beside every conclusion.

sourceBindings.text: Five comparison dimensions

These are tendencies under comparable conditions, not measured field results. Structure, moisture, clay mineralogy, organic matter and profile restrictions can change them. Greater total water held is not all plant-available water.
Dimension
Sandy soil
Loamy soil
Clay-rich soil
Water infiltration
Often very fast
Often moderate
Often slow; cracks may provide fast paths
Total water holding
Often low
Often high
Often very high; not all is available
Cation holding
Often poor
Often good
Often strong; mineralogy and organic matter matter
Aeration
Often good after drainage
Often good with sound structure
Can be poor when wet or dense
Workability
Often easy
Often a favourable balance
Can be sticky when wet and hard when dry

sourceBindings.text: infiltration
Entry of water into soil at the surface; texture and structure both influence it.
leaching
Downward movement of dissolved substances with percolating water, potentially below crop roots.
plant-available water
The portion of stored soil water roots can access under the stated soil and plant conditions; not the same as all retained water.
cation exchange capacity (CEC)
A measure of the capacity to retain exchangeable positively charged ions; affected by clay minerals and organic matter.
soil structure
How soil particles form aggregates and pore spaces; unlike mineral particle-size texture, it can change through management and compaction.
sodicity
A soil chemical condition associated with excessive exchangeable sodium and poor structure; it requires diagnosis rather than inference from clay texture alone.
